section_title: 1.1 The Framework of Time: Financial Year, Previous Year, and
content:
1.1 The Framework of Time: Financial Year, Previous Year, and
Assessment Year
The Indian tax system operates on a structured timeline defined by three key terms: Financial Year
(FY), Previous Year (PY), and Assessment Year (AY). The Financial Year is the 12-month period, run‐
ning from April 1st to March 31st, during which income is earned. For the purposes of this guide, the
relevant Financial Year is FY 2024-25, which commenced on April 1, 2024, and concluded on March 31,
2025. In income tax parlance, this income-earning year is also referred to as the Previous Year, as it
is the year that precedes the year of tax assessment. The Assessment Year is the 12-month period
immediately following the Financial Year, during which the income earned in the Previous Year is as‐
sessed, the tax liability is calculated, and the Income Tax Return (ITR) is filed. Therefore, for income
earned in FY 2024-25 (the Previous Year), the corresponding Assessment Year is AY 2025-26, which
runs from April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026. This sequential relationship ensures that taxpayers have a
complete record of their earnings from a full financial year before the assessment process begins.

section_title: 1.2 Core Income Concepts: Gross Total Income and Total Income
content:
1.2 Core Income Concepts: Gross Total Income and Total Income
Understanding the distinction between Gross Total Income and Total Income is fundamental to the
process of tax calculation. Gross Total Income (GTI) represents the aggregate of all income earned
by a taxpayer during the Previous Year, computed under the five specified heads of income: Income
from Salaries, Income from House Property, Profits and Gains from Business or Profession, Capital
Gains, and Income from Other Sources. GTI is the comprehensive sum of earnings before any deduc‐
tions under Chapter VI-A of the Income Tax Act are applied. It serves as the initial figure from which
the final taxable income is derived. Total Income, on the other hand, is the amount on which the final
tax liability is calculated. It is arrived at by subtracting the eligible deductions from the Gross Total In‐
come. These deductions, primarily available under Chapter VI-A (which includes popular sections like
80C, 80D, etc.), are incentives provided by the government to encourage savings, investments, and
certain expenditures. The final figure, Total Income, is rounded off to the nearest multiple of ten and is
the base for applying the relevant tax slab rates. The availability and extent of these deductions are
heavily dependent on the tax regime—Old or New—chosen by the taxpayer, a critical decision point
that significantly impacts the final tax outgo.

section_title: 1.3 Mandatory ITR Filing Criteria for AY 2025-26
content:
1.3 Mandatory ITR Filing Criteria for AY 2025-26
Filing an Income Tax Return is not optional for all; it becomes a mandatory obligation under several
conditions specified by the Income Tax Act. The primary criterion is the taxpayer’s Gross Total Income.
If an individual’s GTI, before claiming deductions under Chapter VI-A, exceeds the basic exemption lim‐
it for the relevant financial year, filing an ITR is compulsory. For AY 2025-26, this limit is ₹3 lakh under
the default New Tax Regime and varies under the Old Tax Regime based on age (₹2.5 lakh for individu‐
als below 60, ₹3 lakh for senior citizens, and ₹5 lakh for super senior citizens). Beyond this income-
based threshold, several other conditions trigger the mandatory filing requirement, even if the GTI is
below the exemption limit. These rules are designed to ensure greater financial transparency and tax
compliance. An individual must file an ITR if they have deposited an amount or aggregate of amounts
exceeding ₹1 crore in one or more current accounts during the financial year. Similarly, incurring ex‐
penditure exceeding ₹2 lakh for foreign travel for oneself or any other person necessitates filing. An
expenditure of over ₹1 lakh on electricity consumption during the year also makes ITR filing mandat‐
ory. Furthermore, if the total sales, turnover, or gross receipts from a business exceed ₹60 lakh, or if
gross receipts from a profession exceed ₹10 lakh in the previous year, a return must be filed. A signi‐
ficant condition relates to tax deducted or collected at source; if the aggregate amount of TDS and
TCS during the year is ₹25,000 or more (₹50,000 for senior citizens), filing is required. Lastly, any res‐
ident individual who owns foreign assets or has signing authority in a foreign bank account must file
an ITR, regardless of their income level.
Chapter 2: Taxpayer Classification and Residential
Status
The Income Tax Act, 1961, classifies taxpayers into distinct categories, each with specific characterist‐
ics and tax implications. Furthermore, a taxpayer’s residential status in India during a financial year is
a critical determinant of the scope of their taxable income. This chapter explores these classifications
in detail.

2.1 Categories of Taxpayers
Under Section 2(31) of the Income Tax Act, a “person” is defined to include several distinct entities,
each treated as a separate unit for taxation. An Individual refers to a natural human being. This is
the most common category of taxpayer and includes salaried persons, professionals, and small busi‐
ness owners. The tax slabs for individuals are progressive and, under the Old Tax Regime, vary based
on age, with special considerations for senior citizens (60 to 80 years) and super senior citizens (above
80 years). A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) is a unique entity recognized under Hindu law and is
treated as a separate person for tax purposes. It consists of all persons lineally descended from a com‐
mon ancestor and includes their wives and unmarried daughters. A HUF has its own PAN and is taxed
at the same slab rates as an individual. It can claim deductions and exemptions independently of its
members. A Company is an artificial juridical person incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, or
any other law. It has a separate legal identity distinct from its shareholders. Companies are taxed at
flat rates, which differ for domestic and foreign companies. For AY 2025-26, domestic companies are
generally taxed at 25% or 30%, depending on their turnover, while foreign companies face a higher
rate of 40%. A Partnership Firm, including a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP), is an entity
formed by two or more persons who agree to share the profits of a business. For tax purposes, a firm
is assessed as a separate entity. LLPs, governed by the LLP Act, 2008, combine the flexibility of a part‐
nership with the benefit of limited liability for its partners. Both firms and LLPs are taxed at a flat rate
of 30%, plus applicable surcharge and cess. An Association of Persons (AOP) or a Body of Indi‐
viduals (BOI) are entities where two or more persons join together for a common purpose to produce
income. The key distinction is that a BOI can only consist of individuals, whereas an AOP can include
2

non-individuals like companies or firms as its members. The tax treatment of an AOP/BOI depends on
whether the shares of its members are determinate. If shares are unknown, the AOP/BOI is taxed at
the Maximum Marginal Rate. If shares are known, the tax liability is determined based on the income
levels of its members. A Trust is a legal arrangement where a “trustee” holds and manages assets for
the benefit of “beneficiaries.” Trusts can be private (for specific individuals) or public (for charitable or
religious purposes). Public charitable trusts registered under Section 12A/12AA of the Act enjoy signi‐
ficant tax exemptions, provided they apply a specified percentage of their income towards their ob‐
jectives.

2.2 Determination of Residential Status
The residential status of a taxpayer is determined for each financial year and is crucial as it dictates
the scope of income that is subject to tax in India. The status is based on the physical presence of the
individual in India during the relevant year. An individual is considered a Resident in India for a finan‐
cial year if they satisfy at least one of the two basic conditions under Section 6(1): (a) they are in India
for a period of 182 days or more in that year, or (b) they are in India for 60 days or more during that
year AND 365 days or more during the four years immediately preceding that year. For certain indi‐
viduals, such as Indian citizens leaving India for employment or as a crew member of an Indian ship,
the 60-day period in the second condition is extended to 182 days. For Indian citizens or Persons of In‐
dian Origin (PIO) visiting India, this period is extended to 182 days, but is reduced to 120 days if their
total income from Indian sources exceeds ₹15 lakh. A resident individual is further classified as either 
Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) or Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident (RNOR). A
resident becomes an ROR if they satisfy both of the following additional conditions: (a) they have been
a resident in India in at least 2 out of the 10 previous years preceding the relevant year, and (b) their
total stay in India in the 7 previous years preceding the relevant year is 730 days or more. If a resident
individual fails to satisfy one or both of these additional conditions, they are classified as an RNOR.
The RNOR status is also assigned to Indian citizens or PIOs with Indian-sourced income over ₹15 lakh
who stay in India for 120 to 181 days, and to “Deemed Residents.” A Deemed Resident is an Indian cit‐
izen with total income (excluding foreign sources) exceeding ₹15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any
other country. An individual who does not satisfy any of the basic conditions for being a resident is
classified as a Non-Resident (NR) for that financial year.

section_title: 2.3 Tax Implications Based on Residential Status
content:
2.3 Tax Implications Based on Residential Status
The tax implications vary significantly with status. An ROR is taxed on their global income, meaning in‐
come earned in India as well as income earned outside India. An RNOR is taxed on income that is re‐
ceived or accrues in India, and on income from a business controlled from or a profession set up in In‐
dia. Their foreign-sourced income is generally not taxed in India. A Non-Resident is taxed only on the
income that is received, accrues, or is deemed to accrue in India.
Chapter 3: The Five Heads of Income
The Income Tax Act, 1961, under Section 14, mandates the classification of a taxpayer’s income into
five distinct categories or “heads.” This systematic classification is essential for the computation of
Gross Total Income, as each head has its own specific rules for determining taxable income, permiss‐
ible deductions, and applicable exemptions. An item of income can only be taxed under one head.

3.1 Income from Salaries
This is the first and most common head of income, governed by Sections 15 to 17. It covers any remu‐
neration received by an individual from an employer under an employer-employee relationship. The
scope of “salary” is broad and includes wages, pension, annuity, gratuity, fees, commissions, perquis‐
3

ites, profits in lieu of salary, and advance salary. Income is taxable under this head on a “due” or “re‐
ceipt” basis, whichever is earlier. The computation of taxable salary begins with the Gross Salary,
which is the aggregate of all components received from the employer. From this, certain exemptions
and deductions are allowed to arrive at the net taxable salary. Key deductions include the Standard
Deduction, which for AY 2025-26 is ₹50,000 under the Old Regime and ₹75,000 under the New Regime
for salaried individuals and pensioners. Other deductions include Entertainment Allowance (for govern‐
ment employees) and Professional Tax paid. Exemptions for allowances like House Rent Allowance
(HRA) and Leave Travel Allowance (LTA) are available, subject to specific conditions and limits,
primarily under the Old Tax Regime.

3.2 Income from House Property
This head, governed by Sections 22 to 27, deals with the income earned from owning a property,
which could be a building or land appurtenant thereto. The tax is not on the actual rent received but
on the property’s potential to earn income, known as its Annual Value. The computation starts with de‐
termining the Gross Annual Value (GAV), which is the higher of the expected rent (based on municipal
value and fair rent) and the actual rent received or receivable. From the GAV, municipal taxes paid by
the owner are deducted to arrive at the Net Annual Value (NAV). From the NAV, two further deductions
are permitted under Section 24: a standard deduction of 30% of the NAV for repairs and maintenance
(irrespective of actual expenditure), and a deduction for interest paid on capital borrowed for the pur‐
pose of purchase, construction, repair, or reconstruction of the property. For a self-occupied property,
the GAV is taken as nil, but a deduction for interest on a housing loan up to ₹2 lakh can still be
claimed, resulting in a loss from house property that can be set off against other income.

section_title: 3.3 Profits and Gains from Business or Profession (PGBP)
content:
3.3 Profits and Gains from Business or Profession (PGBP)
This head, covered by Sections 28 to 44DB, is the most complex and encompasses income earned
from any trade, commerce, manufacture, profession, or vocation carried on by the taxpayer. The tax‐
able income is the net profit of the business or profession, calculated after deducting all expenses in‐
curred wholly and exclusively for the purpose of that business or profession. The Act provides a com‐
prehensive list of admissible expenses (like rent, repairs, insurance, salaries, depreciation on assets)
and inadmissible expenses (like personal expenses or certain taxes). To simplify compliance for small
taxpayers, the Act also provides for presumptive taxation schemes under Sections 44AD, 44ADA, and
44AE. Under these schemes, income is estimated as a certain percentage of gross turnover or re‐
ceipts, and the taxpayer is not required to maintain detailed books of account. Losses incurred in a
business or profession can be set off against other incomes and can also be carried forward to
subsequent years for set-off.

3.4 Capital Gains
Governed by Sections 45 to 55A, this head covers profits or gains arising from the transfer of a “capit‐
al asset.” A capital asset is defined broadly to include property of any kind, such as real estate, shares,
securities, and gold, though some assets like personal effects are excluded. Capital gains are classified
into two types based on the period for which the asset was held by the taxpayer before its transfer. A 
Short-Term Capital Gain (STCG) arises from the transfer of a short-term capital asset. The holding
period to qualify as short-term varies by asset class (e.g., 12 months for listed securities, 24 months
for immovable property, and 36 months for others). A Long-Term Capital Gain (LTCG) arises from
the transfer of a long-term capital asset. The computation of capital gains involves deducting the cost
of acquisition, cost of improvement, and expenses incurred on transfer from the full value of consider‐
ation received. For LTCG, the taxpayer gets the benefit of “indexation,” where the cost of acquisition
and improvement is adjusted upwards to account for inflation, thereby reducing the taxable gain. Tax
rates for capital gains are specific and differ from slab rates; for instance, STCG on listed equity shares
4

(where STT is paid) is taxed at 15%, while LTCG on the same is taxed at 10% on gains exceeding ₹1
lakh, without indexation. The Act also provides several exemptions from capital gains tax (e.g., under
Sections 54, 54EC) if the sale proceeds are reinvested in specified assets.

3.5 Income from Other Sources
This is a residual head of income, governed by Sections 56 to 59. It covers any income that is not tax‐
able under the other four heads. It is a catch-all category that includes interest income from savings
accounts and fixed deposits, dividend income, winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, and horse
races, gifts received exceeding ₹50,000 from non-relatives, family pension, and income from letting
out machinery or plant along with a building where the two are inseparable. From the gross income
taxable under this head, deductions are allowed for any expenditure incurred for the purpose of earn‐
ing that income. For example, interest paid on a loan taken to make an investment can be deducted
from the interest or dividend income earned from that investment. Family pension is eligible for a
standard deduction of one-third of the pension or ₹15,000, whichever is less.
Chapter 4: Tax Regimes - Old vs New
For the Assessment Year 2025-26, individual taxpayers have the choice between two distinct tax re‐
gimes: the traditional Old Tax Regime and the simplified New Tax Regime under Section 115BAC. The
Finance Act, 2023, made the New Tax Regime the default option. However, taxpayers retain the flexib‐
ility to opt for the Old Regime if it proves more beneficial. The choice is critical as it fundamentally
alters tax rates, available deductions, and overall tax liability.

section_title: 4.1 The Old Tax Regime: A Focus on Deductions
content:
4.1 The Old Tax Regime: A Focus on Deductions
The Old Tax Regime is characterized by its higher tax rates in certain slabs but offers a wide array of
deductions and exemptions that can significantly reduce a taxpayer’s Total Income. This regime is par‐
ticularly advantageous for individuals who make substantial investments in specified tax-saving instru‐
ments and incur eligible expenditures. The income tax slabs under the Old Regime for AY 2025-26 are
differentiated by age. For individuals below 60 years, income up to ₹2,50,000 is exempt; income from
₹2,50,001 to ₹5,00,000 is taxed at 5%; from ₹5,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 at 20%; and income above
₹10,00,000 is taxed at 30%. For senior citizens (60-80 years), the basic exemption limit is ₹3,00,000,
and for super senior citizens (above 80 years), it is ₹5,00,000. The primary appeal of this regime lies
in its extensive list of deductions under Chapter VI-A. This includes the popular Section 80C, which al‐
lows a deduction of up to ₹1.5 lakh for investments in PPF, ELSS, life insurance premiums, and princip‐
al repayment of home loans. Section 80D provides deductions for health insurance premiums, up to
₹25,000 for self and family, with an additional limit for parents. Other significant deductions include
those for interest on education loans (Section 80E) and donations to charitable institutions (Section
80G). Furthermore, exemptions for House Rent Allowance (HRA) and Leave Travel Allowance (LTA) are
available. A tax rebate under Section 87A of up to ₹12,500 is available for resident individuals whose
total income does not exceed ₹5,00,000, effectively making their tax liability zero.

section_title: 4.2 The New Tax Regime (Section 115BAC): Simplicity and Lower
content:
4.2 The New Tax Regime (Section 115BAC): Simplicity and Lower
Rates
The New Tax Regime, the default for AY 2025-26, was introduced to simplify the tax structure by offer‐
ing lower, more streamlined tax rates in exchange for forgoing most of the common deductions and
exemptions. This regime is often more beneficial for taxpayers who do not have significant invest‐
ments or expenditures that qualify for deductions under the Old Regime. The tax slabs under the New
Regime are uniform for all individuals, irrespective of age. For AY 2025-26, income up to ₹3,00,000 is
exempt. Income from ₹3,00,001 to ₹7,00,000 is taxed at 5%; from ₹7,00,001 to ₹10,00,000 at 10%;
5

from ₹10,00,001 to ₹12,00,000 at 15%; from ₹12,00,001 to ₹15,00,000 at 20%; and income above
₹15,00,000 is taxed at 30%. Under this regime, taxpayers must relinquish nearly 70 deductions and
exemptions, including those under Section 80C, 80D, HRA, and LTA. However, a few benefits are re‐
tained. A standard deduction of ₹75,000 from salary and pension income is available. The employer’s
contribution to the National Pension System (NPS) under Section 80CCD(2) is also deductible. A signi‐
ficant feature is the enhanced tax rebate under Section 87A. For resident individuals opting for the
New Regime, if their total income does not exceed ₹7,00,000, they are eligible for a rebate that makes
their tax liability nil. This higher rebate threshold is a key incentive for adopting the new system.

4.3 Comparative Analysis with Examples
The decision of which regime is better depends entirely on an individual’s income level and the
quantum of deductions they can claim. A detailed calculation is necessary to make an informed
choice. For instance, consider a salaried individual under 60 years with a gross salary of ₹12,00,000
who claims deductions for Standard Deduction, Section 80C (₹1,50,000), Section 80D (₹25,000), and
HRA exemption (₹1,00,000). Under the Old Tax Regime, their total income would be ₹8,75,000, leading
to a tax liability of ₹91,000 after cess. Under the New Tax Regime, only the higher standard deduction
of ₹75,000 is allowed, making the total income ₹11,25,000. However, due to the lower slab rates, the
tax liability would be only ₹71,500 after cess. In this scenario, despite high deductions, the New Re‐
gime is more beneficial. In another example, an individual with a gross salary of ₹7,50,000 and no de‐
ductions would have a tax liability of ₹54,600 under the Old Regime. Under the New Regime, their
total income would be ₹6,75,000, which is below the ₹7,00,000 threshold for the enhanced rebate un‐
der Section 87A, resulting in zero tax liability. This clearly demonstrates the superiority of the New
Regime for those with lower incomes and minimal deductions.

4.4 Decision Framework for Regime Selection
The choice between the old and new tax regimes is the most critical tax planning decision for an indi‐
vidual. The optimal choice depends entirely on one’s income level and the quantum of deductions and
exemptions they can claim. The decision should be made after a careful calculation each year. A tax‐
payer should choose the New Regime if their total claimable deductions and exemptions are low, they
do not have major expenses like high rent (HRA) or a home loan, they prefer simplicity, or they are in
the early stages of their career. Conversely, a taxpayer should choose the Old Regime if they can
claim significant exemptions like a high HRA, have a substantial home loan interest component, fully
utilize investment limits under Sections 80C, 80D, and 80CCD(1B), or have an ongoing education loan.
Ultimately, the choice is personal and dynamic. A taxpayer might find the new regime beneficial one
year and the old regime better the next, depending on changes in their financial situation. An annual
review is essential for optimal tax planning. Taxpayers without business income can switch between
regimes each year when filing their return, allowing them to choose the most advantageous option
based on their financial situation for that specific year.
Chapter 5: Deductions Under Chapter VI-A
Chapter VI-A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, offers a suite of deductions that allow taxpayers to reduce
their Gross Total Income (GTI), thereby lowering their overall tax liability. These deductions are
primarily available to taxpayers who opt for the old tax regime.

section_title: 5.1 Section 80C: The Cornerstone of Tax Savings
content:
5.1 Section 80C: The Cornerstone of Tax Savings
Section 80C, along with its sub-sections 80CCC and 80CCD(1), provides a consolidated deduction limit
of up to ₹1,50,000 per financial year. This section encourages long-term savings and investments
through a variety of eligible instruments and expenses. A key condition is that these deductions are
6

exclusively available under the old tax regime. A wide array of investments are eligible under this
section. The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a popular choice, offering a 15-year lock-in period and
an Exempt-Exempt-Exempt (EEE) status. For salaried individuals, contributions to the Employees’
Provident Fund (EPF) are a mandatory and effective way to utilize this limit. For those with a higher
risk appetite, Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS) offer a compelling option with a mandatory
lock-in period of just three years. Insurance products also feature prominently, with premiums paid for
life insurance policies for oneself, spouse, or children being eligible. Certain expenditures also qualify
for deduction. Tuition fees paid for the full-time education of up to two children in any recognized
educational institution in India are deductible. For homeowners, the principal repayment compon‐
ent of a home loan is a significant eligible expense. Government-backed savings schemes like the 
National Savings Certificate (NSC), Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY), Tax-saver Fixed De‐
posits, and the Senior Citizens Savings Scheme (SCSS) are other secure avenues.

5.2 Section 80CCC and Section 80CCD: Pension Contributions
Section 80CCC allows for a deduction on contributions made to specific pension funds or annuity plans
offered by insurance companies, falling within the overall ₹1,50,000 limit of Section 80C. Section
80CCD is dedicated to contributions to the National Pension System (NPS) and is divided into
three crucial sub-sections. Section 80CCD(1) covers contributions made by an employee or a self-
employed individual, limited to 10% of salary for salaried individuals and 20% of gross total income for
the self-employed, also clubbed within the overall ₹1.5 lakh limit. A significant additional benefit
comes from Section 80CCD(1B), which provides an exclusive deduction of up to ₹50,000 for contri‐
butions to NPS, over and above the combined ₹1.5 lakh limit, effectively allowing a total deduction of
up to ₹2,00,000. This additional deduction is only available under the old tax regime. Furthermore, 
Section 80CCD(2) pertains to the employer’s contribution to an employee’s NPS account. Under the
old regime, this is capped at 10% of salary for private-sector employees and 14% for central govern‐
ment employees. A key update for FY 2024-25 is that under the new tax regime, a deduction of up to
14% of salary is available for all employees, making it a valuable tax-saving tool in both regimes.

section_title: 5.3 Section 80D: Health Insurance and Medical Expenditure
content:
5.3 Section 80D: Health Insurance and Medical Expenditure
Section 80D provides deductions for health insurance premiums and certain medical expenses, avail‐
able only under the old tax regime. For an individual below 60 years of age, a deduction of up to
₹25,000 is allowed for premiums paid for self, spouse, and dependent children. An additional deduc‐
tion of up to ₹25,000 is available for premiums paid for parents below 60 years of age. If the parents
are senior citizens (60 years or older), this additional deduction limit increases to ₹50,000. If the indi‐
vidual or their spouse is a senior citizen, the primary deduction limit also increases to ₹50,000. There‐
fore, a taxpayer can claim a maximum deduction of up to ₹1,00,000 if both the taxpayer (or spouse)
and their parents are senior citizens. Within these limits, a deduction of up to ₹5,000 for preventive
health check-ups is also permitted. Furthermore, if senior citizen parents are not covered by any
health insurance, medical expenditure incurred for them up to ₹50,000 can be claimed as a deduction.

section_title: 5.4 Section 80DD and Section 80U: Support for Persons with
content:
5.4 Section 80DD and Section 80U: Support for Persons with
Disabilities
Section 80DD offers a fixed deduction to a resident individual or HUF for the maintenance, including
medical treatment, of a dependent with a disability. The deduction is not linked to the actual amount
spent. A flat deduction of ₹75,000 is available for a dependent with a normal disability (40% to 80%),
which increases to ₹1,25,000 for a severe disability (80% or more). The dependent can be a spouse,
child, parent, or sibling. Section 80U provides a similar deduction for the taxpayer themselves if they
suffer from a disability. The deduction amounts are identical: ₹75,000 for normal disability and
7

₹1,25,000 for severe disability. Both 80DD and 80U require a valid medical certificate (Form 10-IA) and
are available only under the old tax regime.

5.5 Section 80DDB: Treatment of Specified Diseases
This section allows a deduction for medical expenses incurred for the treatment of specified diseases
for the taxpayer or a dependent relative. The list of diseases includes neurological ailments, malignant
cancers, AIDS, chronic renal failure, and hematological disorders. The deduction is limited to the actual
expenditure or a specified amount, whichever is lower. For individuals below 60 years, the limit is
₹40,000. For senior citizens (60 years or older), the limit is ₹1,00,000. Any amount reimbursed by an
insurer or employer must be subtracted from the claimable amount. This deduction is exclusive to the
old tax regime.

5.6 Section 80E: Interest on Education Loan
Section 80E provides a deduction for the interest paid on a loan taken for higher education. There is 
no upper limit on the amount of interest that can be claimed as a deduction. The loan can be for the
taxpayer, their spouse, children, or a student for whom the taxpayer is a legal guardian. The deduc‐
tion is available for a maximum of eight consecutive years, starting from the year the interest repay‐
ment begins. Only the interest component is deductible, not the principal. This benefit is available only
under the old tax regime.

section_title: 5.7 Section 80EE and 80EEA: Interest on Home Loan for First-Time
content:
5.7 Section 80EE and 80EEA: Interest on Home Loan for First-Time
Buyers
These sections provided additional deductions on home loan interest for first-time homebuyers, over
and above the ₹2 lakh limit under Section 24. Section 80EE was applicable for loans sanctioned
between April 1, 2016, and March 31, 2017, offering an additional deduction of up to ₹50,000. Sec‐
tion 80EEA applied to loans sanctioned between April 1, 2019, and March 31, 2022, for affordable
housing (property value up to ₹45 lakh), offering an additional deduction of up to ₹1,50,000. While
new loans are no longer eligible, taxpayers with existing loans sanctioned within these periods can
continue to claim these deductions under the old tax regime until their loan tenure ends.

5.8 Section 80G: Donations to Charitable Institutions
Section 80G allows deductions for donations made to specified funds and charitable institutions. The
deductions are categorized based on the recipient and are subject to different limits. Donations to
funds like the Prime Minister’s National Relief Fund and the National Defence Fund are eligible for a 
100% deduction without any qualifying limit. Donations to funds like the Jawaharlal Nehru Me‐
morial Fund and the Rajiv Gandhi Foundation qualify for a 50% deduction without any qualifying
limit. Other donations, such as those to government-approved institutions for promoting family
planning, are eligible for a 100% deduction subject to a qualifying limit of 10% of the adjusted
gross total income. Most other donations to registered charitable institutions fall under the category of 
50% deduction subject to the 10% qualifying limit. Donations exceeding ₹2,000 must be made
through modes other than cash.

5.9 Other Key Deductions (80GG, 80TTA, 80TTB, 80GGC)
Several other sections under Chapter VI-A cater to specific situations. Section 80GG provides relief
for rent paid by individuals who do not receive House Rent Allowance (HRA). The deduction is the
minimum of ₹5,000 per month, 25% of total income, or rent paid minus 10% of total income. Section
80TTA allows a deduction of up to ₹10,000 on interest earned from savings bank accounts for
individuals (below 60 years) and HUFs. For senior citizens, Section 80TTB provides a much larger de‐
duction of up to ₹50,000 on interest income from all types of deposits, including savings accounts,
8

fixed deposits, and recurring deposits. Section 80GGC allows a 100% deduction for contributions
made to a political party or an electoral trust. Sections 80IA to 80IE offer profit-linked deductions for
businesses engaged in infrastructure, power generation, and industrial undertakings in specific re‐
gions, though most of these have sunset clauses and are not available for new businesses.
Chapter 6: Exemptions Under Section 10
Section 10 of the Income Tax Act lists various types of income that are exempt from tax. Unlike deduc‐
tions, which reduce Gross Total Income, exemptions are incomes that are not included in the
computation of total income in the first place.

6.1 Key Exemptions for Individuals
The Income Tax Act provides several exemptions that are crucial for individual taxpayers, particularly
those who are salaried. These exemptions reduce the taxable income at the source level itself, before
the calculation of Gross Total Income. The availability of many of these exemptions is a key differenti‐
ating factor between the old and new tax regimes, with most being available only under the old re‐
gime. Understanding these provisions is essential for effective salary structuring and tax planning.

6.2 Agricultural Income (Section 10(1))
Income derived from agricultural land in India is fully exempt from tax under Section 10(1). This ex‐
emption is available in both the old and new tax regimes. However, there is a specific method of cal‐
culation if an individual’s net agricultural income exceeds ₹5,000 and their total non-agricultural in‐
come exceeds the basic exemption limit. In such cases, the agricultural income is aggregated with the
non-agricultural income for the purpose of determining the tax rate applicable to the non-agricultural
income. This method, known as the partial integration of taxes, ensures that while the agricultural in‐
come itself is not taxed, it can push the non-agricultural income into a higher tax slab, thereby
increasing the overall tax liability.

6.3 House Rent Allowance (Section 10(13A))
For salaried individuals receiving House Rent Allowance (HRA) from their employer, a portion of this al‐
lowance is exempt from tax under Section 10(13A), provided they live in rented accommodation. This
is one of the most significant tax-saving components for the salaried class and is available only under
the old tax regime. The amount of exemption is calculated as the minimum of three figures: the actual
HRA received from the employer, the actual rent paid for the accommodation minus 10% of the salary,
or 50% of the salary for those living in metropolitan cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata) and 40%
for those in non-metropolitan cities. For this calculation, ‘salary’ includes the basic salary and dearness
allowance (if it forms part of retirement benefits), but excludes other allowances and perquisites.

6.4 Leave Travel Allowance (Section 10(5))
Leave Travel Allowance (LTA) or Leave Travel Concession (LTC) is another tax exemption available to
salaried employees under the old tax regime. This exemption covers the cost of travel incurred by an
employee and their family for journeys within India during a leave period. The exemption is available
for two journeys in a block of four calendar years. The amount of exemption is limited to the actual
travel fare incurred, subject to certain conditions. For instance, if the journey is by air, the exemption
is limited to the economy class airfare of the national carrier by the shortest route. If the journey is by
rail, it is limited to the AC first-class rail fare. The exemption does not cover expenses related to
accommodation, food, or local conveyance.
9

6.5 Retirement Benefits
Several exemptions are provided for amounts received at the time of retirement, offering financial
relief to individuals ending their professional careers. Under Section 10(10), gratuity received by
government employees is fully exempt from tax. For non-government employees covered under the
Payment of Gratuity Act, the exemption is limited to the least of the actual amount received, ₹20 lakh,
or 15 days’ salary for each completed year of service. Section 10(10A) provides an exemption for
the commuted (lump-sum) portion of a pension. For government employees, it is fully exempt. For oth‐
ers, one-third of the total pension is exempt if they also receive gratuity, and one-half is exempt if they
do not. Section 10(10AA) deals with leave encashment at retirement. For government employees, it
is fully exempt. For non-government employees, the exemption limit has been substantially increased
to ₹25 lakh from FY 2024-25. Compensation received under a Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)
is exempt up to ₹5 lakh under Section 10(10C). These exemptions are generally available in both tax
regimes.

6.6 Special Allowances (Section 10(14))
Section 10(14) provides exemptions for various special allowances granted by an employer to an em‐
ployee. These are available only under the old tax regime. The allowances are broadly divided into two
categories. The first category includes allowances granted to meet expenses wholly, necessarily, and
exclusively incurred in the performance of official duties. The exemption for these is limited to the
amount actually spent. This includes allowances like travel allowance, daily allowance, conveyance al‐
lowance, helper allowance, academic allowance, and uniform allowance. The second category includes
allowances granted to meet personal expenses. These are exempt up to a specified limit, irrespective
of the actual amount spent. This category includes Children Education Allowance, which is exempt up
to ₹100 per month per child for a maximum of two children, and Hostel Expenditure Allowance, which
is exempt up to ₹300 per month per child for a maximum of two children.
Chapter 7: Tax-Saving Investment Options
Choosing the right tax-saving instruments is crucial for effective financial planning. The choice de‐
pends on an individual’s risk appetite, financial goals, and liquidity needs. Most of these investment
options provide deductions only under the old tax regime.

7.1 Public Provident Fund (PPF)
The Public Provident Fund (PPF) is a government-backed, long-term savings scheme with a 15-year
lock-in period. It is an extremely low-risk instrument and is highly favored for its Exempt-Exempt-Ex‐
empt (EEE) status, which means the amount invested, the interest earned, and the maturity proceeds
are all completely tax-free. The interest rate is set by the government quarterly and for the first
quarter of FY 2024-25, it stands at 7.1%. PPF is an ideal choice for conservative investors who are
looking for a secure, long-term investment for goals such as retirement or children’s education. The
investment qualifies for deduction under Section 80C.

section_title: 7.2 Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) and Voluntary Provident
content:
7.2 Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) and Voluntary Provident
Fund (VPF)
The Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) is a mandatory retirement savings scheme for salaried employ‐
ees in the organized sector. The employee’s contribution (typically 12% of basic salary) is eligible for
deduction under Section 80C. The interest earned on the EPF balance is also largely tax-free, with the
current rate for FY24 being 8.25%. It is a very low-risk option with low liquidity, as withdrawals are
generally restricted until retirement. The Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF) is an extension of the EPF, al‐
lowing employees to contribute more than the mandatory 12% of their salary towards their provident
10

fund account. VPF contributions also qualify for the 80C deduction and earn the same high, tax-free
interest as EPF, making it an excellent tool for accelerating retirement savings.

7.3 Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS)
Equity Linked Savings Schemes (ELSS) are diversified equity mutual funds that come with a tax bene‐
fit under Section 80C. They have the shortest mandatory lock-in period among all 80C instruments,
which is just three years. ELSS funds invest primarily in the stock market, which means they carry a
high market risk but also have the potential to generate significantly higher returns over the long
term, historically in the range of 12-15%. They are suitable for investors with a higher risk tolerance
and a medium to long-term investment horizon who are looking for wealth creation along with tax sav‐
ings. Long-term capital gains from ELSS are taxed at a concessional rate of 10% on gains exceeding
₹1 lakh in a financial year.

7.4 National Pension System (NPS)
The National Pension System (NPS) is a market-linked, voluntary retirement savings scheme regulated
by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA). It offers a unique tax-saving
structure. Employee contributions up to 10% of salary are deductible under Section 80CCD(1) within
the overall ₹1.5 lakh limit of 80C. Additionally, it offers an exclusive deduction of up to ₹50,000 under
Section 80CCD(1B), which is over and above the 80C limit. The employer’s contribution is also deduct‐
ible under Section 80CCD(2). NPS carries a medium level of risk as the returns are linked to the per‐
formance of equity and debt markets. It has very low liquidity, with a lock-in until the age of 60,
making it a disciplined tool for long-term retirement planning.

7.5 Tax-Saving Fixed Deposits
Tax-saving Fixed Deposits (FDs) are a simple and low-risk investment option offered by banks and post
offices that qualify for deduction under Section 80C. They come with a mandatory lock-in period of five
years, and premature withdrawal is not permitted, ensuring very low liquidity. The returns are modest,
typically in the range of 6-7%, and are fixed at the time of investment. A significant drawback is that
the interest earned on these FDs is fully taxable at the investor’s applicable slab rate, which reduces
the post-tax yield, making them less attractive compared to other EEE instruments like PPF.

7.6 National Savings Certificate (NSC)
The National Savings Certificate (NSC) is a 5-year post office savings scheme backed by the Govern‐
ment of India. It is a very low-risk instrument with a fixed interest rate, which is currently 7.7% for the
first quarter of FY 2024-25. The investment in NSC qualifies for deduction under Section 80C. A unique
feature of NSC is that the interest accrued each year is deemed to be reinvested and also qualifies for
the 80C deduction (except for the final year’s interest). However, the entire interest income is taxable
at maturity. It offers no liquidity before the 5-year maturity period.

7.7 Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY)
The Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (SSY) is a government-backed savings scheme designed for the finan‐
cial security of a girl child. It can be opened for a girl child below the age of 10. The scheme offers a
high, tax-free interest rate (currently 8.2%) and enjoys the EEE status, making the investment, in‐
terest, and maturity amount all tax-free. The annual contributions, up to ₹1.5 lakh, are eligible for de‐
duction under Section 80C. It has a long lock-in period, maturing 21 years from the date of account
opening, making it a suitable long-term investment for goals like the child’s higher education and mar‐
riage.
11

7.8 Life Insurance and ULIPs
Premiums paid for life insurance policies for oneself, spouse, or children are eligible for deduction un‐
der Section 80C. Traditional life insurance plans, such as endowment and money-back policies, offer
low returns (typically 4-6%) but provide the dual benefit of life cover and savings. Unit Linked Insur‐
ance Plans (ULIPs) are a combination of insurance and investment. They are market-linked and offer
the potential for higher returns (8-10%) but also carry a medium level of risk. The maturity proceeds
from life insurance policies are generally tax-free under Section 10(10D), subject to certain conditions
regarding the premium-to-sum-assured ratio.
Chapter 8: ITR Forms and Selection
The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) notifies a set of seven ITR forms, each designed for a specific
category of taxpayer based on their sources of income, the quantum of income, and their legal status.
Selecting the correct form is the foundational step of the filing process, as an incorrect choice can lead
to the return being classified as ‘defective’.

8.1 Understanding the Seven ITR Forms
For the Assessment Year 2025-26, the Income Tax Department has notified seven distinct Income Tax
Return forms, namely ITR-1, ITR-2, ITR-3, ITR-4, ITR-5, ITR-6, and ITR-7. Each form is tailored to a spe‐
cific class of taxpayer, ensuring that the information collected is relevant to their financial profile. The
forms range from the very simple ITR-1 (Sahaj) for small salaried taxpayers to the highly complex
ITR-6 for companies. The selection of the appropriate form is not a matter of choice but a mandatory
requirement based on the taxpayer’s status and the nature of their income. The forms are updated an‐
nually to incorporate legislative changes from the Union Budget and to enhance the scope and clarity
of disclosures required from taxpayers.

8.2 ITR-1 (Sahaj)
ITR-1, also known as Sahaj, is the simplest of all ITR forms, designed for resident individuals with a rel‐
atively straightforward income profile. Its primary objective is to reduce the compliance burden for a
large segment of the salaried class and pensioners. To be eligible to file ITR-1, a taxpayer must be a
Resident Individual (not ‘Not Ordinarily Resident’) whose total income for the financial year does not
exceed ₹50 lakh. The permissible sources of income are strictly defined and include income from
salary or pension, income from one house property (excluding cases with brought-forward losses), and
income from other sources such as interest from savings accounts, fixed deposits, and family pension.
Additionally, agricultural income up to ₹5,000 is permitted. An individual cannot use this form if they
are a director in any company, have held unlisted equity shares, have any income from business or
profession, or have foreign assets or income.

8.3 ITR-2
ITR-2 is designed for Individuals and Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) who are not eligible to file ITR-1
and do not have any income under the head “Profits and Gains of Business or Profession.” This form is
significantly more detailed than ITR-1 and accommodates a wider range of income sources and com‐
plex financial situations. There is no upper limit on the total income for filing ITR-2. It is the appropriate
form for salaried individuals or pensioners who have income from capital gains, own more than one
house property, have foreign assets or foreign income, or have agricultural income exceeding ₹5,000.
It is also the designated form for individuals who are directors in a company or have investments in
unlisted equity shares. Taxpayers who need to carry forward losses from previous years under the
heads ‘Income from House Property’ or ‘Capital Gains’ must use ITR-2.
12

8.4 ITR-3
ITR-3 is applicable to Individuals and HUFs who have income from a proprietary business or from carry‐
ing on a profession. This form is one of the most comprehensive and complex ITR forms, as it requires
the filer to furnish detailed financial statements, including a Profit and Loss account and a Balance
Sheet. It caters to taxpayers who earn income from sources such as salary, house property, capital
gains, and other sources, in addition to their business or professional income. There is no income
threshold for filing ITR-3. It is the mandatory form for individuals who are partners in a partnership
firm, as the income from the firm (including salary, interest, and share of profit) is reported here. Any
individual or HUF whose income is subject to a tax audit under Section 44AB must file ITR-3.

8.5 ITR-4 (Sugam)
ITR-4, also known as Sugam, is a simplified return form for individuals, HUFs, and Partnership Firms
(other than LLPs) who have opted for the presumptive taxation scheme under Sections 44AD, 44ADA,
or 44AE of the Income Tax Act. This scheme allows small taxpayers to declare income at a prescribed
rate of their turnover or gross receipts, thereby relieving them from the tedious task of maintaining
detailed books of account. The total income of the taxpayer must not exceed ₹50 lakh to be eligible
for ITR-4. The form can be used by resident individuals, HUFs, and firms. In addition to presumptive
business income, ITR-4 can be used to report income from salary or pension, one house property, and
other sources, similar to ITR-1. However, a taxpayer cannot use ITR-4 if they are a director in a com‐
pany, have held unlisted equity shares, have foreign assets or income, or own more than one house
property.

8.6 ITR-5
ITR-5 is designed for entities other than individuals, HUFs, companies, and persons filing ITR-7. It is a
specific form applicable to a diverse group of taxpayers, including Partnership Firms, Limited Liability
Partnerships (LLPs), Association of Persons (AOPs), Body of Individuals (BOIs), Artificial Juridical Persons
(AJPs), estates of the deceased, estates of the insolvent, business trusts, and investment funds. This
form requires the filer to provide detailed information about their income from various sources, includ‐
ing business or profession, and must be accompanied by financial statements like the Balance Sheet
and Profit and Loss Account. All entities filing ITR-5 are required to file their returns electronically, with
the option of using a digital signature.

8.7 ITR-6
ITR-6 is the designated income tax return form exclusively for companies registered under the Indian
Companies Act, 2013, or any other previous company law. The only exception is for companies that
claim an exemption under Section 11, which pertains to income from property held for charitable or
religious purposes; such companies are required to file ITR-7. ITR-6 must be filed electronically and
must be verified using a Digital Signature Certificate (DSC). There is no option for paper filing or veri‐
fication through other electronic means. This form is highly detailed and requires companies to report
extensive information related to their financial statements, including the Balance Sheet, Profit and
Loss Account, and various audit reports. It includes specific schedules for computing Minimum
Alternate Tax (MAT) under Section 115JB.

8.8 ITR-7
ITR-7 is a specialized form for persons, including companies, who are required to furnish their return
under specific sections of the Income Tax Act, namely Sections 139(4A), 139(4B), 139(4C), 139(4D),
139(4E), or 139(4F). This form is primarily used by trusts, political parties, and other institutions that
claim exemptions on their income. The categories of filers include charitable or religious trusts, politic‐
al parties, scientific research associations, news agencies, hospitals, and universities. The form re‐
13

quires detailed reporting of income, application of income for charitable or religious purposes, and
details of donations received.

8.9 Choosing the Correct ITR Form
Selecting the appropriate ITR form is a critical first step that dictates the accuracy and validity of the
entire tax filing process. The e-filing portal of the Income Tax Department offers an intuitive wizard-
based service named “Help me decide which ITR form to file” that guides taxpayers through a series
of questions to arrive at the correct form. The process begins by identifying the taxpayer’s category
(Individual, HUF, Company, etc.) and then delves into the sources of income. For individuals and HUFs,
the key differentiator is the presence of business or professional income, which narrows the choice to
ITR-3 or ITR-4. If there is no business income, the choice is between ITR-1 and ITR-2, based on factors
like total income exceeding ₹50 lakh, having multiple house properties, capital gains, or foreign as‐
sets. Filing an incorrect ITR form can lead to the return being treated as ‘defective’ under Section
139(9), which can result in penalties, loss of the ability to carry forward losses, and delays in receiving
refunds. If a mistake is made, it can be corrected by filing a ‘Revised Return’ under Section 139(5)
before the specified deadline.
Chapter 9: ITR Filing Procedures and Compliance
The ITR filing process can be broken down into three distinct phases: pre-filing preparation, the actual
filing of the return, and post-filing compliance. A systematic approach to each phase is essential for a
smooth and error-free experience.

9.1 Pre-Filing Preparation
Thorough preparation is the cornerstone of accurate tax filing. This phase involves registering on the
e-filing portal, gathering all necessary documents, and understanding the key tax statements that
provide the data for your return. Before you can file your ITR online, you must be registered on the of‐
ficial Income Tax e-filing portal (incometax.gov.in). This one-time process involves validating your PAN,
providing basic personal and contact details, verifying them through OTPs sent to your mobile and
email, and setting a secure password. Once registered, you can log in using your PAN as the User ID.

9.2 Portal Registration Guide
Before you can file your ITR online, you must be registered on the official Income Tax e-filing portal (in‐
cometax.gov.in). Registration is a one-time process. First, navigate to the portal and click the “Re‐
gister” button. You will need to enter your Permanent Account Number (PAN) and validate it. After val‐
idation, you must fill in your basic personal details as they appear on your PAN card, such as your full
name and date of birth. The next step requires you to provide a valid mobile number and email ad‐
dress, which are crucial for receiving One-Time Passwords (OTPs) and all future communications. The
portal will send separate OTPs to your mobile and email for verification. Once verified, you will set a
secure password for your account and a personalized secure access message. After completing these
steps, your registration is successful, and you can log in to your e-filing account.

9.3 Required Documents Checklist
Before you begin filling out your ITR form, it is crucial to have all the relevant documents and informa‐
tion organized. While you do not need to attach any documents with your return, you are legally re‐
quired to retain them. The core documents include your PAN Card and Aadhaar Card. For income
proof, you will need Form 16 from your employer, Form 16A for non-salary TDS, bank statements for
interest income, rental agreements, and capital gains statements from your broker. For claiming de‐
ductions and exemptions, you must have investment proofs for Section 80C (like PPF receipts, ELSS
14

statements), health insurance premium receipts for Section 80D, donation receipts for Section 80G,
and home loan interest certificates. You should also have challans for any advance tax or self-
assessment tax paid during the year.

9.4 Understanding Form 26AS, AIS, and TIS
The Income Tax Department provides three critical statements that consolidate your financial and tax-
related information. It is mandatory to review and reconcile these statements with your own records
before filing your ITR. Form 26AS is your annual tax credit statement, showing all TDS, TCS, and
advance tax paid against your PAN. The Annual Information Statement (AIS) is a more compre‐
hensive statement displaying a wide array of financial information reported by various entities,
including salary, interest, dividends, and property and security transactions. The Taxpayer Informa‐
tion Summary (TIS) is a category-wise summary of the information in the AIS. It is crucial to ensure
that the income and tax details reported in your ITR match the information in these statements to
avoid discrepancies and potential notices from the department.

9.5 Filing Methods: Online and Offline
The department offers two modes for filing: online and offline. The online method is suitable for ITR-1
and ITR-4 and involves filling and submitting the form directly on the e-filing portal. After logging in,
you select the assessment year and filing mode, and the portal guides you through the pre-filled form,
which you need to verify, complete, and submit. The offline method is available for all ITR forms and is
particularly useful for complex returns like ITR-2 and ITR-3. This method involves downloading an ‘ITR
Offline Utility’ from the portal, filling the form on your computer, and then uploading the generated
JSON file to the portal. This allows you to work on your return offline and is less prone to internet
connectivity issues.

section_title: 9.6 Section-by-Section Guide for Key ITR Forms
content:
9.6 Section-by-Section Guide for Key ITR Forms
Filing a detailed form like ITR-2 requires careful attention to its various schedules. In Schedule S
(Salary), you must report salary, perquisites, and exempt allowances as per your Form 16, and claim
deductions under Section 16 like the standard deduction. Schedule CG (Capital Gains) is one of the
most complex sections, requiring asset-wise details of sale price, cost of acquisition (indexed for
LTCG), and any exemptions claimed under sections like 54 or 54F. It has a specific sub-schedule, 
Schedule 112A, for reporting scrip-wise details of LTCG on listed equity. Schedule VI-A is where you
claim all your deductions under Chapter VI-A, such as those under Section 80C for investments, Sec‐
tion 80D for health insurance, and Section 80E for education loan interest. Each claim must be backed
by valid proof.

9.7 Post-Filing Compliance and E-Verification
Submitting your ITR is not the final step. The process is only complete once you have verified your re‐
turn. Verification is the act of confirming that the information furnished in the return is true and cor‐
rect. An unverified return is treated as invalid. As per the revised rules, taxpayers are required to e-
verify their ITR within 30 days of filing it. The department offers multiple electronic methods for veri‐
fication, eliminating the need to physically send a signed copy of the ITR-V acknowledgement to the
CPC in Bengaluru. The most common methods include using an Aadhaar OTP, logging in through Net
Banking, using a Digital Signature Certificate (DSC), or generating an Electronic Verification
Code (EVC) through a pre-validated bank or Demat account.

9.8 Types of Tax Returns
The Income Tax Act provides for different types of returns to be filed under various circumstances. The 
Original Return (Section 139(1)) is the standard return filed for the first time within the due date. If a
15

taxpayer misses the due date, they can file a Belated Return (Section 139(4)) before the end of the
assessment year, but this attracts a late fee and loss of the right to carry forward certain losses. If an
error is discovered in the original return, a Revised Return (Section 139(5)) can be filed to correct it,
which completely replaces the original return. A newer provision, the Updated Return (ITR-U) (Sec‐
tion 139(8A)), allows taxpayers a longer window of 24 months from the end of the assessment year to
declare any income they missed reporting, but this involves paying an additional tax.

9.9 Key Compliance Deadlines for AY 2025-26
Adhering to deadlines is a critical aspect of tax compliance. For AY 2025-26, the primary due date for
individuals and entities whose accounts are not required to be audited has been extended to Septem‐
ber 16, 2025. For taxpayers who are required to get their accounts audited (like companies and
certain businesses/professionals), the due date for filing the ITR is October 31, 2025, with the tax
audit report due by September 30, 2025. For taxpayers with international transactions requiring a
transfer pricing report, the due date is November 30, 2025. The last date to file a belated or revised
return for AY 2025-26 is December 31, 2025. Missing these dates can lead to financial penalties and
other legal consequences.
Chapter 10: Special Cases and Complex Scenarios
This chapter delves into the specific tax provisions and compliance requirements for various complex
situations and categories of taxpayers, including Non-Resident Indians, transactions involving capital
gains, business and professional income, and special considerations for senior citizens.

10.1 NRI Taxation
The taxation of a Non-Resident Indian (NRI) is fundamentally determined by their residential status,
which is based on their physical presence in India during a financial year. An NRI is taxed only on in‐
come that is earned or received in India, such as salary for services rendered in India, rental income
from Indian property, and capital gains on assets located in India. Their foreign income is not taxable
in India. NRIs manage their finances through NRO, NRE, and FCNR accounts. Interest on NRO accounts
is taxable, while interest on NRE and FCNR accounts is tax-free. To prevent double taxation, NRIs can
avail benefits under the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between India and their coun‐
try of residence. TDS is deducted at higher rates on payments to NRIs, for instance, 30% on NRO in‐
terest and 20% on long-term capital gains from property. An NRI must file an ITR in India if their Indian
income exceeds the basic exemption limit.

10.2 Capital Gains Taxation
Capital gains tax is levied on the profit from the sale of a capital asset. The tax treatment depends on
the holding period, which classifies the gain as either Short-Term Capital Gain (STCG) or Long-Term
Capital Gain (LTCG). The holding period varies by asset class: over 12 months for listed equity, over 24
months for property, and over 36 months for assets like gold. STCG is generally taxed at slab rates
(15% for listed equity), while LTCG is taxed at concessional rates (10% on listed equity gains over ₹1
lakh, 20% on property and gold). For LTCG on assets like property, the benefit of indexation is avail‐
able, which adjusts the purchase cost for inflation, reducing the taxable gain. The Act provides several
exemptions under sections like 54, 54F, and 54EC if the gains or sale proceeds are reinvested in spe‐
cified assets. Losses from capital assets can be set off and carried forward as per specific rules.

10.3 Business and Professional Income
Income earned from any trade, commerce, or profession is taxed under the head “Profits and Gains of
Business or Profession” (PGBP). The taxable income is computed by adjusting the net profit as per the
16

profit and loss account for various allowances and disallowances prescribed in the Income Tax Act. Ex‐
penses incurred wholly and exclusively for the business are deductible, while personal or capital ex‐
penses are disallowed. To simplify compliance for small taxpayers, the Act provides presumptive taxa‐
tion schemes under Section 44AD (for businesses), Section 44ADA (for professionals), and Section
44AE (for transporters), where income is presumed to be a certain percentage of turnover or receipts,
eliminating the need for detailed bookkeeping. A tax audit by a Chartered Accountant is mandatory
under Section 44AB if the turnover or gross receipts exceed specified limits.

10.4 Freelancers and Gig Workers
Freelancers and gig workers are treated as self-employed individuals, and their earnings are taxable
under the head “Profits and Gains of Business or Profession.” They can deduct all expenses incurred
for their work, such as internet bills, software subscriptions, and a portion of home rent if used as an
office. They can opt for the presumptive taxation scheme under Section 44ADA (if their work is a spe‐
cified profession, with income presumed at 50% of receipts) or Section 44AD (if it is a business, with
income presumed at 6-8% of turnover). Clients are required to deduct TDS on payments to freelancers
under Section 194J (10% for professional fees) or 194C. Since there is no monthly tax deduction, freel‐
ancers are liable to pay advance tax in quarterly installments if their annual tax liability exceeds
₹10,000.

10.5 Real Estate Transactions
The sale of real estate results in capital gains, taxed as STCG (if held for ≤ 24 months) at slab rates or
LTCG (if held for > 24 months) at 20% with indexation. The buyer of a property worth ₹50 lakh or more
is required to deduct TDS at 1% under Section 194-IA. Significant tax exemptions are available on
LTCG under Section 54 (if gains from a residential property are reinvested in another residential prop‐
erty) and Section 54F (if sale proceeds from any asset are invested in a residential property), subject
to a maximum investment cap of ₹10 crore. Rental income from property is taxed under “Income from
House Property,” allowing for a standard deduction of 30% and a deduction for home loan interest.

10.6 Foreign Assets and Income Reporting
All Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) individuals are required to report their foreign assets and
income in their ITR. This is done in Schedule FA (Foreign Assets), which requires disclosure of foreign
bank accounts, financial interests, immovable property, and other assets held abroad. This reporting is
mandatory regardless of the asset’s value. Failure to disclose can attract a steep penalty of ₹10 lakh
under the Black Money Act. Furthermore, undisclosed foreign assets, when discovered, are taxed at
30% with a penalty of 90% of the asset’s value, leading to a total liability of 120%. International agree‐
ments like FATCA and CRS enable automatic exchange of financial information between countries,
making it extremely difficult to hide foreign assets.

section_title: 10.7 Senior Citizens and Super Senior Citizens
content:
10.7 Senior Citizens and Super Senior Citizens
The Income Tax Act provides several benefits for elderly taxpayers. Under the old tax regime, senior
citizens (60-80 years) have a higher basic exemption limit of ₹3 lakh, and super senior citizens (80+
years) have a limit of ₹5 lakh. They are eligible for a higher deduction of up to ₹50,000 for health in‐
surance premiums under Section 80D. A key benefit is the deduction of up to ₹50,000 on interest in‐
come from all deposits under Section 80TTB. Senior citizens without business income are also exempt
from paying advance tax. These benefits are designed to reduce the tax burden and simplify
compliance for the elderly.

17

Chapter 11: Penalties, Notices, and Appeals
This chapter outlines the penal provisions for non-compliance with income tax laws, the various types
of notices issued by the tax department, and the process for appealing against an assessment order.

11.1 Penalties and Consequences
Non-compliance with income tax laws attracts various penalties. Delay in filing the ITR leads to in‐
terest under Section 234A and a late filing fee of up to ₹5,000 under Section 234F. Non-payment or
short payment of advance tax attracts interest under Sections 234B and 234C. Underreporting of in‐
come can lead to a penalty of 50% of the tax payable on such income, while misreporting of income
attracts a harsher penalty of 200% under Section 270A. In severe cases of willful tax evasion, the de‐
partment can initiate prosecution, which may lead to imprisonment. Not filing an ITR also results in the
inability to carry forward losses. Failure to link PAN with Aadhaar renders the PAN inoperative, leading
to higher TDS rates and an inability to file returns.

11.2 Tax Notices and Assessments
The Income Tax Department communicates with taxpayers through various notices. An intimation
under Section 143(1) is a preliminary assessment after the ITR is processed, which may result in a
demand or refund. A notice under Section 143(2) is issued to select a case for detailed scrutiny, re‐
quiring the taxpayer to produce evidence to support their claims. A notice under Section 148 is is‐
sued to reopen a past assessment if the Assessing Officer believes some income has escaped
taxation. A demand notice under Section 156 is issued to collect any outstanding tax, interest, or
penalty. It is crucial to respond to these notices accurately and within the specified time limit, usually
through the e-filing portal.

11.3 Appeal Process
If a taxpayer is aggrieved by an order of the Assessing Officer, they have a right to appeal. The first
level of appeal is to the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) [CIT(A)], which must be filed within 30
days of receiving the order. If the taxpayer is not satisfied with the CIT(A)’s decision, a further appeal
can be made to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), which is the final fact-finding authority. Bey‐
ond the ITAT, appeals can be filed with the High Court and then the Supreme Court, but only if they in‐
volve a substantial question of law. This hierarchical process provides a mechanism for dispute
resolution and ensures that taxpayers have recourse against incorrect assessments.

11.4 Settlement Commission and Dispute Resolution
The Income Tax Settlement Commission (ITSC) was an alternative dispute resolution body where tax‐
payers could apply for settlement of their tax disputes, offering a chance to disclose additional income
and seek immunity from penalty and prosecution. However, the ITSC has been discontinued for new
applications since February 1, 2021. An Interim Board for Settlement has been constituted to handle
pending cases. The government has been focusing more on other dispute resolution mechanisms like
the faceless appeal scheme to enhance transparency and reduce litigation.
Chapter 12: Tax Planning and Optimization Strategies
Effective tax planning is a year-round activity, not a last-minute scramble in March. It involves stra‐
tegic structuring of salary, timely investments, and making informed decisions to maximize savings.
18

12.1 Year-Round Tax Planning
A structured approach to tax planning begins at the start of the financial year in April. This is the time
to choose between the old and new tax regimes and communicate this to your employer for appropri‐
ate TDS deduction. Investments should be planned and executed systematically. For instance, starting
a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) in an ELSS fund in April allows for better averaging of costs. Mid-
year, around September-October, is a good time to review your investments against your declarations
and make any necessary adjustments. The last quarter (January-March) should be for finalizing invest‐
ments and submitting proofs to the employer, avoiding the rush and potential for poor decisions.

12.2 Salary Structuring for Tax Efficiency
Under the old regime, structuring your salary to include tax-efficient components can lead to signific‐
ant savings. Maximizing components like House Rent Allowance (HRA) and Leave Travel Allowance
(LTA) is key. Negotiating for reimbursements for expenses like telephone bills, internet, and newspa‐
pers, instead of taxable allowances, can also reduce your tax outgo. The employer’s contribution to
NPS under Section 80CCD(2) is a valuable component available in both regimes and should be utilized.

12.3 Tax-Efficient Withdrawal Strategies
For retirees, planning withdrawals is as important as planning investments. The sequence of withdraw‐
al can impact tax liability. It is generally advisable to first withdraw from tax-free sources like PPF and
EPF. Next, one can realize long-term capital gains from equity, which are taxed at a concessional rate.
Interest income from fixed deposits can be planned to utilize the ₹50,000 deduction available to senior
citizens under Section 80TTB. Annuity and pension income, which are fully taxable, should be drawn
last.

12.4 Common Mistakes to Avoid
A common mistake is investing in sub-optimal products solely for tax-saving purposes, without consid‐
ering financial goals or risk profile. For example, mixing insurance and investment by buying low-re‐
turn endowment plans is often inefficient. Another error is focusing only on Section 80C and ignoring
other valuable deductions like Section 80D for health insurance or the additional NPS benefit under
80CCD(1B). Procrastinating until the last minute often leads to hasty decisions. Finally, many taxpay‐
ers assume the old regime is always better and fail to perform an annual comparison with the new
regime, potentially losing out on tax savings.

12.5 Regime-Specific Analysis and Break-Even Points
The choice between the old and new tax regimes is the most critical tax planning decision. The optim‐
al choice depends entirely on one’s income level and the quantum of deductions. For lower incomes
(up to ₹10 lakh), the new regime is often more beneficial due to the enhanced rebate and higher
standard deduction. At a ₹10 lakh salary, the break-even point is around ₹2.25 lakh in deductions; if
deductions are less than this, the new regime is better. For mid-range incomes (₹15 lakh), the break-
even point for deductions is around ₹5.62 lakh. For higher incomes (₹30 lakh and above), the old re‐
gime starts to become more advantageous, provided the taxpayer can claim substantial deductions.
At a ₹30 lakh income, the break-even point is around ₹8.5 lakh in deductions. Taxpayers must perform
this break-even analysis annually to make an informed decision.
